title: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy
objective: After this level you can explain how the Great Law of Peace joined five nations into one league, and why its influence on the US Constitution is debated.
summary: The Peacemaker and Hiawatha joined five nations under the Great Law of Peace: 50 chiefs chosen by Clan Mothers, unanimous decisions. Whether it shaped the US Constitution is still argued.

cards.headline: Five nations buried their weapons under a tree, then recorded it in beads.
cards.body: That’s the founding story of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. It is also the start of an argument about the US Constitution.

cards.headline: The People of the Longhouse
cards.body: Haudenosaunee means “People of the Longhouse.” The five original nations were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca. Their tradition credits the Peacemaker, helped by Hiawatha, with uniting them under the Great Law of Peace. The Hiawatha Belt records the moment the warring nations buried their weapons under the Tree of Peace, in Onondaga territory. Wampum beads are white and purple shell, and a belt’s design is a memory aid for history and laws: a constitution you can hold.

cards.headline: How the League decided
cards.body: Under the Great Law, 50 peace chiefs shared authority, each nation had one vote, and decisions had to be unanimous. Each nation’s chiefs are chosen by Clan Mothers. In 1722 the Tuscarora joined, and the English began calling the league the Six Nations. Even its birthday is debated: many scholars say the 1400s, some as late as about 1600, and others argue for 1142, the year of a solar eclipse that may match a sign in the sky in the oral tradition.

cards.headline: The colonists were watching
cards.body: At a 1744 treaty meeting, the Onondaga leader Canassatego urged the colonies to unite. In 1751 Benjamin Franklin argued that if the Six Nations could form such a union, a dozen English colonies should manage one too. In 1988, on the Constitution’s 200th anniversary, Congress passed a resolution acknowledging the contribution of the Iroquois Confederacy and other Indian nations to the United States.

cards.headline: How historians weigh it
cards.body: Historians still argue about how far the influence went. Donald Grinde and Bruce Johansen argue that Iroquois and other Native political ideas helped shape American government, including the Constitution. Skeptics answer that European political theory supplied the Founders’ models and that the evidence for Native influence is thin.

mascot.line: Notice the move: the events of 1744, 1751 and 1988 are settled. The argument is about what they add up to.
